title.en: Glooskap Names the Animals and Forms His Family
title.zh: 格魯斯卡普為百獸命名並建立家室

region.en: Land of the Wabanaki, nearest to the sunrise (Maine and the Maritimes)
region.zh: 最接近日出的瓦巴納基之地（緬因與加拿大沿海）

texts.period: Passamaquoddy tradition recorded by Charles G. Leland (1884)

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'Of the Great Deeds which Glooskap did for Men'

summary.en: Glooskap comes over the sea in a great stone canoe, an island of granite covered with trees, and names the animals: the Bear fears man, the Squirrel - greater than the Bear in those days - is smoothed down to his present size and becomes Glooskap's dog, and the Moose and Beaver confess they would flee or run. Seeing that of all created beings the first and greatest was Man, he teaches men - who lived in darkness - how to hunt, build huts and canoes and weirs, the virtues of plants and roots, and the names of all the stars. He dwells with Noogumee his grandmother and Abistarnoock the Martin, who can change himself from baby to youth, and who wears the magic belt of endless strength when Glooskap lends it.
summary.zh: 格魯斯卡普乘巨石之舟——覆滿樹木的花崗岩島——渡海而來，為百獸命名：熊懼人，松鼠（彼時比熊還大）被他撫小至今日的模樣，成為其獵犬；麋鹿與河狸皆自承要逃。他見人是造物之首，便教導處於黑暗的人類狩獵、築屋、造舟結網、辨識草木之性，並為群星命名。他與「祖母」諾古米同住，又有能自由變身大小的貂弟阿比斯塔諾克，佩上主人的法帶便力大無窮。

sensitivity.note: Passamaquoddy tradition (Leland 1884); public domain. Leland prints the Indian-English manuscript with editorial notes.

passages.text: It is told in traditions of the old time that Glooskap was born in the land of the Wabanaki, which is nearest to the sunrise; but another story says that he came over the sea in a great stone canoe, and that this canoe was an island of granite covered with trees. When the great man, of all men and beasts chief ruler, had come down from this ark, he went among the Wabanaki. And calling all the animals he gave them each a name: unto the Bear, mooin; and asked him what he would do if he should meet with a man. The Bear said, 'I fear him, and I should run.' Now in those days the Squirrel (mi-ko) was greater than the Bear. Then Glooskap took him in his hands, and smoothing him down he grew smaller and smaller, till he became as we see him now.
passages.note: Condensed from Leland 1884, pp. 28-29; not verbatim.

passages.text: In after-days the Squirrel was Glooskap's dog, and when he so willed, grew large again and slew his enemies, however fierce they might be. But this time, when asked what he would do should he meet with a man, Mi-ko replied, 'I should run up a tree.' Then the Moose, being questioned, answered, standing still and looking down, 'I should run through the woods.' And so it was with Kwah-beet the Beaver, and Glooskap saw that of all created beings the first and greatest was Man.
passages.note: Condensed from Leland 1884, pp. 29-30; not verbatim.

passages.text: Before men were instructed by him, they lived in darkness; it was so dark that they could not even see to slay their enemies. Glooskap taught them how to hunt, and to build huts and canoes and weirs for fish. Before he came they knew not how to make weapons or nets. He, the Great Master, showed them the hidden virtues of plants, roots, and barks, and pointed out to them such vegetables as might be used for food, as well as what kinds of animals, birds, and fish were to be eaten. And when this was done he taught them the names of all the stars. He loved mankind, and wherever he might be in the wilderness he was never very far from any of the Indians: he dwelt in a lonely land, but whenever they sought him they found him.
passages.note: Condensed from Leland 1884, p. 30; not verbatim.

passages.text: Glooskap was never married, yet as he lived like other men he lived not alone. There dwelt with him an old woman, who kept his lodge; he called her Noogumee, 'my grandmother.' With her was a youth named Abistarnoock, or the Martin. And Martin could change himself to a baby or a little boy, a youth or a young man, as befitted the time in which he was to act; for all things about Glooskap were very wonderful. This Martin ate always from a small birch-bark dish, and when he left this anywhere Glooskap was sure to find it, and could tell from its appearance all that had befallen his family. And Martin was called by Glooskap Uch-keen, 'my younger brother.' The Lord of men and beasts had a belt which gave him magical power and endless strength; and when he lent this to Martin, the younger brother could also do great deeds, such as were only done in old times.
passages.note: Condensed from Leland 1884, pp. 30-31; not verbatim.

title.en: Glooskap Pursues the Sorcerer Win-pe, and the Whale Smokes a Pipe
title.zh: 格魯斯卡普追捕巫師溫佩，鯨魚吸菸斗

region.en: From the St. John River to Newfoundland along the Wabanaki coasts
region.zh: 自聖約翰河沿岸至紐芬蘭的瓦巴納基海岸

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'How Win-pe the Sorcerer... and how the Whale smoked a Pipe'

summary.en: The sorcerer Win-pe carries off Glooskap's grandmother and the Martin, and Glooskap rests seven years before pursuing. He sings the magic song the whales obey, rejects the small whale that sinks under one foot, and rides the mighty female toward the coast; she fears shoal water, and the Clams - his deadly enemies - sing to her to throw off and drown the rider, but Glooskap mistranslates their chant as 'hurry him along,' and she runs herself high on the shore. Singing her forgiveness he pushes her off with his bow, gives her an old pipe and tobacco, and stands on the shore watching the long low cloud that follows her until she vanishes in the far away.
summary.zh: 巫師溫佩擄走祖母與貂弟；格魯斯卡普獨居七年方启程追索。他高唱馭鯨之歌，先來的小鯨不堪其一足之重而遭遣回；得巨鯨負他渡海。鯨懼擱淺，而他的死敵蛤蜊在沙下合唱，教鯨把乘者甩下水去；格魯斯卡普卻把蛤歌「譯」作「快些趕路」，鯨遂全速衝上灘頭。主人唱起饒恕之歌，以弓輕推送她回深海，又賜老菸斗與菸草；他立於岸上，遠望她吐出的低雲伴她沒入天涯。

passages.text: In old times, in the beginning of things, men were as animals and animals as men... they could change to one or the other form; yet even as men there was always something which showed what they were. Now Glooskap lived on an island named Aja-lig-un-meehk, and with him were many Indians with the names and natures of animals and birds. These men, but most of all Pulowech, the Partridge, having acquired power themselves, became jealous of Glooskap, and made up their minds to depart when he was away, taking with them Martin and the grandmother... he returned home and found the old woman, whose name was Mooinarkw (Mrs. Bear), and Martin had been taken away. Following their tracks to the shore he saw one of his greatest enemies, a terrible sorcerer named Win-pe, just pushing off in his canoe. And with him were his wife and child and Dame Bear and Martin.
passages.note: Condensed from Leland 1884, pp. 31-32; not verbatim.

passages.text: But Glooskap rested seven years alone before he pursued the enemy, though some say it was seven months. And when the time had come, he took his dogs and went to the shore, and looked far out to sea over the waves, and sang the magic song which the whales obey. Soon there rose in the distance a small whale, who had heard the call, and came to Glooskap; but he was then very great, and he put one foot on the whale to test his weight, and the fish sank under him. So he sent it away. Then the lord of men and beasts sang the song again, and there came the largest, a mighty female, and she bore him well and easily over to Kes-poog-itk. But she was greatly afraid of getting into shoal water, or of running ashore.
passages.note: Condensed from Leland 1884, pp. 33-34; not verbatim.

passages.text: She saw shells below, and soon the water grew so shoal that she said in fear, 'Does not the land show itself like a bow-string?' And he said, 'We are still far from land.' Then the water grew so shoal that she heard the song of the Clams as they lay under the sand, singing to her that she should throw him off and drown him; for these Clams were his deadly enemies. But Bootup the Whale did not understand their language, so she asked her rider - for he knew Clam - what they were chanting to her. And he replied in a song: 'They tell you to hurry, to hurry, to hurry him along, over the water, away as fast as you can!' Then the Whale went like lightning, and suddenly found herself high on the shore. Then she lamented and sang: 'Alas, my grandchild, ah, you have been my death; I can never leave the land, I shall swim in the sea no more.'
passages.note: Condensed from Leland 1884, p. 34; not verbatim.

passages.text: But Glooskap sang: 'Have no fear, noogumee, you shall not suffer, you shall swim in the sea once more.' Then with a push of his bow against her head he sent her off into deep water, and the Whale rejoiced greatly. But ere she went she said, 'Oh, my grandson, hast thou not such a thing as an old pipe and some tobacco?' He replied, 'Ah yes. You want tobacco, I behold you.' So he gave her a short pipe and some tobacco, and thereunto a light. And the Whale, being of good cheer, sailed away, smoking as she went, while Glooskap, standing silent on the shore, and ever leaning on his maple bow, beheld the long low cloud which followed her until she vanished in the far away.
passages.note: Condensed from Leland 1884, pp. 34-35; not verbatim.

title.en: The Evil Pitcher: Witch of the Enchanted Sausages and the Giant Flight
title.zh: 邪惡的罐婆：魔法香腸與巨人追逐

region.en: Grand Manan and the Wabanaki coast, Bay of Fundy
region.zh: 芬迪灣的格蘭馬南島與瓦巴納基海岸

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'Of the Dreadful Deeds of the Evil Pitcher'

summary.en: The witch Pook-jin-skwess, the Pitcher, falls in love with the young Glooskap and pursues him in giant form - like the wind chasing the cloud, the lightning chasing the thunder - until he leaps nine miles from the mainland to Grand Manan; her long pointed snowshoe-marks are seen deep in the rocks to this day. On his pursuit of Win-pe she guards the road as a filthy trembling hag crawling with devil-vermin; Glooskap picks each imp from her hair, turns them to porcupines and toads, crushes a cranberry for the noise, and lets her wake mocked. At the sorcerer's lodge her daughters offer enchanted sausages to string about his neck; his dogs - told 'Stop!' in a word they know as 'At them!' - tear the witches, and the master strangles the old man with his own sausage-links.
summary.zh: 巫婆「罐婆」坡吉斯奎絲愛上年輕的格魯斯卡普而化形追逐——如風逐雲、電逐雷——直至他從大陸一躍九里登上格蘭馬南島；她那尖長雪鞋的印痕至今深嵌岩石。格魯斯卡普追索溫佩途中，她扮作遍生魔鬼蟲的醜嫗守路；他逐一從她髮間拈出小鬼，使之化為豪豬與蟾蜍，捏碎蔓越莓裝作捏蟲，戲弄而過。在巫師屋中，其女以魔法香腸作項圈相贈；他的犬聽見他喊「住口」（犬卻聽成「撲上去」），撕碎眾巫，主人以香腸鏈絞殺老巫。

sensitivity.note: Passamaquoddy tradition (Leland 1884); public domain. Leland notes the witch may have given her name to Moll Pitcher of Lynn.

passages.text: When Glooskap came into the world it abounded in giants, monsters, sorcerers and witches, fiends and devils. Among the witches there was one whom the Passamaquoddy call Pook-jin-skwess, or the Pitcher. And they have a legend that she once fell in love with Glooskap when he was young and had not gained the power of his riper age. He fled before her, and she pursued him. It was a dreadful flight, since to make rapid steps both took the form of giants by their m'teoulin, or magic power. It was like an awful storm in winter, the wind chasing the cloud; it was like a frightful tempest in summer, the lightning chasing the thunder. As the snow lay deep, both had snow-shoes on. When they came to the shore Glooskap leaped from the main-land to the island of Grand Manan, and so escaped her. Now the snow-shoes of Glooskap were sumsook, or round, while those of Pook-jin-skwess were long and pointed, and the marks of them as they jumped are to be seen deep in the rocks to this day.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, p. 36; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: And when he came to Ogumkeok he found a hut, and in it, seated over a fire, the ugliest old hag he had ever seen, trembling in every limb, as if near death, dirty, ragged, and loathsome in all ways. Looking up at him with bleared eyes, she begged him to gather her a little firewood, which he did. And then she prayed him to free her from the vermin with which she was covered, and which were maddening her with their bites. These were all devils in disguise, the spirits of foul poison, such as she deemed must kill even the Master. Now Glooskap, foreseeing all this, had taken with him, as he came, from a bog many cranberries. And bidding Pook-jin-skwess bend over, he began to take from her hair the hideous vermin, and each, as he took it, became a horrid porcupine or toad. Then the hag asked, 'Have you found one?' 'I have,' replied the Master. 'Crush it!' was her answer, and Glooskap crushed a cranberry; and she, hearing the noise, thought that he had done as she bid, and that the poison on his fingers would penetrate to his life.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 38-39; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: The girls came out greeting him with very pleasant glances, wooing softly and sweetly; they offered him a string of sausages... But these which the girls offered, as girls do, to show their love, by casting the string round the neck of the favored youth, were enchanted, and had they once put the necklace upon him he would have been overpowered. However, they knew not of this new magic which the Master had brought into the land, by which one can read the heart... When his dogs growled at them he cried, 'Cuss!' which means Stop! but which the dogs only knew as 'Hie, at them!' So they flew at the witches, and these flashed up like fire into their own dreadful forms of female fiends. Then there was a terrible tumult, for never before in the land of the Wabanaki had there been such a battle... Then he entered the wigwam where the old sorcerer sat, waiting for him as food. And the Master said, 'Are you hungry? Or do you love sausages? Here they are!' Instantly casting the links around his neck, he was taken, and Glooskap slew him with one blow.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 40-41; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: Pook-jin-skwess and the Black Cats: The Birth of the Mosquito
title.zh: 罐婆與黑貓族：蚊蟲之誕生

region.en: Black Cat village and Bar Harbor, Maine coast
region.zh: 黑貓族村與緬因州的巴港

texts.period: Passamaquoddy version told by Noel Josephs, recorded by Leland (1884)

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'How the Story of Glooskap and Pook-jin-skwess is told by the Passamaquoddy Indians'

summary.en: In a village of Black Cats, the chief Pogumk (Glooskap) feeds all the people; the witch Pitcher - a Black Cat, man or woman as she willed - strands him on an egg-gathering island and paddles home singing 'I shall be the chief of the Fishers now.' The Fox, hearing his magic song from beyond the mountains, swims him home with the warning to hold his tail in good faith; the chief, of little faith, opens an eye - and ten feet become ten miles against Pitcher's storm. Back in camp he has Sable burn the witch's babe; as she pursues like a starving wolf, he confronts her and magically pins her back against a tree, where the Black Cats mock her all night as she chops herself free. Fleeing to Bar Harbor she wishes to become something to torment all men - and becomes the mosquito.
summary.zh: 黑貓族村中，酋長波恭克（格魯斯卡普）養活全族；女巫罐婆——同族、可男可女——把他騙上採蛋的荒島，划舟而歸，且行且歌：「今後我便是漁者之酋。」狐聽見他遠山的魔法歌，泅水來渡；囑他閉眼抱尾、信之勿疑；酋長心存疑慮偷眼一開——十呎化作十里，逆著罐婆掀起的风暴。回村後他命貂弟焚巫婆之嬰；罐婆如餓狼追來，他迎面現身，以法術將她釘在樹上，黑貓族人徹夜譏笑她劈木自脫。她逃至巴港，咒願化為折磨眾人之物——便成了蚊子。

sensitivity.note: Passamaquoddy version (Leland 1884); public domain. The infanticide is villain-vs-villain story register.

passages.text: There was a village of Indians who were all Black Cats, or Po'gum'k. One of them, the cleverest and bravest, went forth every day with bow and arrow, tomahawk and knife, and killed moose and bear, and sent meat to the poor, and so he fed them all... Pook-jin-skwess, the Witch, was a Black Cat. She was a woman or a man as she willed to be; but in these days she was a man. And she, being evil, hated the chief, and thought long how she could kill or remove him, and take his place. Now, one day when all the camp had packed what they had, being about to travel, Pitcher asked the chief to go with him... down to the water-side to gather gulls' eggs. And then they went far out in a canoe... till they came to an island, and there they landed, and while Pogumk (who was Glooskap) sought for eggs, the false-hearted Pitcher stole away in the canoe, and as she paddled she sang a song: 'I have left the Black Cat on an island, I shall be the chief of the Fishers now!'
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 44-45; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Now on the thirtieth day the chief remembered his friend the Fox, who had m'teoulin, or magic power. And he sang a song, and the Fox heard it, although he was miles away, beyond forests and mountains. And thus knowing all, he went to the shore and swam to the island, where he found the chief... The Fox said, 'Close thine eyes and hold fast to my tail as tightly as thou canst, and be of good faith, oh, my elder brother, and we shall soon gain the shore.' Saying this, he swam away and his friend followed. And it went well with them, but the chief grew weary, and he opened one eye a little, and saw that they were not ten feet from the shore. And being of little faith he thought, 'We shall never get to land.' But the Fox replied, 'Do not believe it.' But the journey lasted long, for what seemed to Pogumk to be ten feet was ten miles, and the wind was high and the waters were wild, for Pitcher had called forth a storm. So they swam all day and all the evening before they landed.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 46-47; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: And the chief bade Sable run to the camp. 'And when you are there, build up a great fire of hemlock bark, and take Pitcher's babe, even the babe which she loves, and which you tend, and throw it into the fire, and run to me as fast as you can... And as he commanded it was done; and when the fire was hot, Sable threw the babe into it, and it was burned to death. And Pitcher, being, as one may well believe, maddened at such a sight, pursued him as a starving wolf pursues a rabbit... And at that word Pogumk stepped forward and confronted her, and said, 'Truly, she need not run so far.' And seeing him and hearing this, fear came upon her; but she laughed aloud to hide it... Then, as his magic had come to him, he used his power, and put Pitcher with her back against a tree; and there she stayed, stuck to it, unable to get away. But the chief and Sable went to the camp. Now Pitcher had a hatchet and wedge, and with much ado she cut herself away, and the Black Cats heard her pounding and chopping all night long. And in the morning she came to them, and there was a great piece of wood sticking to her back, and they laughed her to scorn.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 47-48; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Now Pitcher the Witch, being mad with shame and spite, fled from the face of man, and ran through the woods like a wild wolf. And so she came to Bar Harbor, and sat down on a log, and said, with her heart full of bitterness and malice, 'I would that I could become something which should torment all men.' And as she said this she became a mosquito (T'sis-o), and so it came to pass that mosquitoes were made. And to this day men see that wherever the Black Cat is, there too is the Sable not far away.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, p. 49; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: Glooskap and the Loons: His Faithful Messengers
title.zh: 格魯斯卡普與潛鳥：忠實的信使

region.zh: 紐芬蘭（烏克圖坎庫）的湖泊

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'How Glooskap became friendly to the Loons'

summary.en: Pursuing Win-pe, Glooskap sees from afar the Loons flying over water, circling the lake thrice as if seeking something; their chief would be his servant and friend. Glooskap teaches him a strange long cry like the howl of a dog, to be uttered when the loons need him; and in Newfoundland he comes to a town of Loons in human form who rejoice to see their lord, and he makes them his huntsmen and messengers. Whence to this day, when the Indians hear the cry of the Loon, they say, 'Kwemoo el-komik-too-ujul Gloocapcil' - He is calling upon Glooskap.
summary.zh: 追索溫佩途中，格魯斯卡普遠望潛鳥在水上盤旋三匝，似有所求；鵝首自願為其僕友。格魯斯卡普授牠一種如犬吠般的奇異長鳴，有需則呼。其後他在紐芬蘭來到一座全是化形潛鳥的城鎮，眾鳥歡迎其主；他便立牠們為自己的獵手與信使。故至今印第安人聞潛鳥長鳴，便說：「牠在呼喚格魯斯卡普。」

passages.text: When Glooskap was pursuing Win-pe, he one day on Uktukamkw saw from afar flying over water the Kwe-moo, or Loons. And thrice did their chief make the circle of the lake, coming near to the land of men and beasts every time, as if he would fain seek somewhat. Then Glooskap asking him what he wanted, Kwe-moo replied that he would be his servant and friend. So Glooskap taught him a strange long cry like the howl of a dog, and when the loons were in need of him or would pray to him they were to utter this cry.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, p. 50; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: And it came to pass that when he was in Newfoundland he came to an Indian town, and they who dwelt therein were all Kwee-moo-uk, or Loons. And they, as men, were exceeding glad to see their lord, who had blessed them as birds, and did their best to please him. So he made them his huntsmen and messengers, and in all the tales of Glooskap the Kwee-moo ever appears as faithful to him. Whence to this day, when the Indians hear the cry of the Loon, they say, 'Kwemoo el-komik-too-ujul Gloocapcil' (He is calling upon Glooskap).
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 50-51; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: Glooskap Makes a Great Man of His Uncle Mikchich the Turtle
title.zh: 格魯斯卡普使龜叔米基奇成為偉人

region.en: Piktook (Pictou), Nova Scotia, and its lake
region.zh: 新斯科舍的皮克托及其湖泊

texts.period: Micmac and Passamaquoddy traditions compiled from six versions by Leland (1884)

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'How Glooskap made his Uncle Mikchich the Turtle into a Great Man'

summary.en: Poor, lazy, not very clever old Mikchich the Turtle bears all his wants with such good nature that Glooskap resolves to make of him a mighty man: with the magic belt he becomes young and comely, marries the loveliest daughter of the chief of Piktook, and is warned that the jealous young men will trample him at the ball game - jump the lodge twice, but the third time is terrible. Caught on the tent-poles in the smoke, he is smoked into his hard shell and made the sogmo, great chief of the Tortoises, able to roll through flame, live on land or water, and survive his own severed head for nine days. Thrown into a fire he sleeps and calls for more wood; begged-and-prayed not to be drowned, he fights them lustily - is thrown in the lake - and next noon is found basking on a rock, saying 'Good-by,' and rolling over plump into the water, where he is living to this day; and in memory of Glooskap's jest the Turtle layeth eggs even to this day.
summary.zh: 貧窮懶惰、其貌不揚的龜叔米基奇性情溫厚，格魯斯卡普決意使他成為偉人：繫上法帶他便年少俊美，娶得皮克托酋長最美的小女兒，又受警在球賽中會被妒忌的少年踐踏——跳屋兩次可脫，第三次必有凶險。他第三次果然被帳頂煙霧中的椽木掛住；主人以菸將他薰成堅殼，立他為龜族大酋長——可穿火而行、水陸兩棲、斷首九日不死。投之於火，他酣睡醒來討柴；眾人商議溺斃，他佯作驚恐苦苦哀求——被拋入湖中——次日正午卻見他曝於岩上，說聲「再見」，翻身撲通入水，至今仍在；為紀念此趣，龜自那日起產卵至今。

sensitivity.note: Leland 1884; public domain. Totem-origin story of the Tortoise, highest rank among the Algonquin clans.

passages.text: And this was not because this man, whose name in Micmac is Mikchich and in Passamaquoddy Chickwe-notchk, meaning the Turtle, was great, or well favored, or rich. For truly he was none of these, being very poor and lazy, no longer young, and not very clever or wise in any way. It is said that he was indeed Glooskap's uncle, but others think that this was by adoption. However, this old fellow bore all his wants with such good nature that the Master, taking him in great affection, resolved to make of him a mighty man... Glooskap, being a very handsome, stately man, with the manner of a great chief, was much admired, and that not a little by all the women, so that every one wished to have him in the house. Yet he gave them all the go-by, and dwelt with his old uncle, in whose quaint ways and old-time stories he took great delight.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 52-53; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: 'Truly, if that be all, uncle,' replied Glooskap, 'I trow I can turn tailor and fit you to a turn... for to him who knows how, 't is as easy to make a man over as a suit of clothes.' 'Yes; but, nephew,' said Mikchich, 'how say you as to making over the inside of a mortal?' 'By the great Beaver!' answered the Master, 'that is something harder to do, else I were not so long at work in this world. But before I leave this town I shall do that also for you; and as for this present sport, do but put on my belt.' And when he had done that, Mikchich became so young and handsome that no man or woman ever saw the like... So Mikchich went to the feast. Now the chief of Piktook had three beautiful daughters, and the youngest was the loveliest in the land. And on her he cast his eyes, and returning said, 'I have seen one whom I want.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 53-54; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: All this happened as he foretold; for the young men indeed tried to take his life, and to escape them Mikchich jumped over the lodge, so that he seemed like a bird flying. But the third time he did this he was caught on the top of the tent-poles, and hung there dangling in the smoke which rose from below. Then Glooskap, who was seated in the tent, said, 'Uncle, I will now make you the sogmo, or great chief of the Tortoises, and you shall bear up a great nation.' Then he smoked Mikchich so long that his skin became a hard shell, and the marks of the smoke may be seen thereon to this day... And he cried aloud, 'Miloohs! My nephew, you will kill me!' But the nephew replied, 'Not so. I am giving you great life. From this time you may roll through a flame and never feel it, and live on land or in the water. And though your head be cut off, it will live for nine days, and your heart, even, shall beat as long when taken from your body.' So Mikchich rejoiced greatly.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 55-56; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: And they seized him and threw him into a great fire, but he turned over and went to sleep in it, being very lazy; and when the fire had burnt out he awoke, and called for more wood, because it was a cold night. Then they seized him yet again, and spoke of drowning. But, hearing this, he, as if he were in mortal dread, begged them not to do this thing. And he said they might cut him to pieces, or burn him, as they would, but not to throw him into the water. Therefore they resolved to do so, and dragged him on. Then he screamed horribly and fought lustily, and tore up trees and roots and rocks like a madman; but they took him into a canoe and paddled out into the middle of the lake, and, throwing him in, watched him sink as he vanished far down below. So they thought him dead, and returned rejoicing. Now the next day at noon there was a hot sunshine, and something was seen basking on a great rock, about a mile out in the lake... And when they came to the edge of the rock... there lay Mikchich sunning himself; but seeing them coming to take him, he only said, 'Good-by,' and rolled over plump into the water, where he is living to this day. In memory whereof all turtles, when they see any one coming, tip-tilt themselves over into the water at once.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 56-57; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: Glooskap Vanquishes a Sorcerer by Smoking Tobacco
title.zh: 格魯斯卡普以吸菸鬥敗巫師

region.en: The Wabanaki land where tobacco was once raised
region.zh: 曾種菸草的瓦巴納基之地

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'Of Turtles' Eggs, and how Glooskap vanquished a Sorcerer by smoking Tobacco'

summary.en: The great Glooskap was a right valiant smoker; in all the world was no man who loved a pipe of good tobacco so much as he. In those days the summers were longer, the sun was warmer, and the Indians raised tomawe (tobacco). An evil-minded magician, believing himself greatest in all things, sought to appall Glooskap by outdoing him at something at which he excelled - for a fish is frightened when another swims faster, but not till then. The sorcerer sat down to smoke with an exceeding long pipe with a great bowl, but that of Glooskap grew much greater; the sorcerer burnt his out at one pull and blew all the smoke from his nose at one puff. Glooskap, whose pipe held ten times as much tobacco, did the same, and blowing it out split the rocky ground, so that a great chasm opened before them. 'If you can do that you may kill me.' But he could not, and went back with shame to those who had sent him.
summary.zh: 偉大的格魯斯卡普是出了名的老菸槍，普天之下無人比他更愛一斗好菸。那時夏天更長、日頭更暖，印第安人種著菸草。一位自詡天下第一的惡巫想在他最擅長的事上壓倒他——魚只有在別人游得更快時才會驚惶。巫師以超長大斗菸對坐較量，格魯斯卡普的菸斗卻脹得更大；巫師一口吸盡、一鼻噴盡；格魯斯卡普的菸斗容得十倍之菸，如法炮製，噴氣之間竟劈裂岩地，一道深壑在他們面前裂開。「你能如此，便可以殺我。」巫師做不到，羞慚而返。

passages.text: The great Glooskap was a right valiant smoker; in all the world was no man who loved a pipe of good tobacco so much as he. In those days the summers were longer in the land of the Wabanaki, the sun was warmer, and the Indians raised tomawe (tobacco), and solaced themselves mightily therewith. And there came to Glooskap a certain evil-minded magician, who sought to take his life, as the Master very well knew, for he read the hearts of men as if they had been strings of wampum. And this m'teoulin, believing himself to be greatest in all things, thought to appall Glooskap by outdoing him at first in something at which he excelled; for a fish is frightened when another swims faster, but not till then.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 58-59; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: And the man sat down to smoke with an exceeding long pipe with a great bowl, but that of Glooskap grew to be much greater. Then, having filled his pipe, the sorcerer exhausted and burnt it out at one pull, and then blew all the smoke out of his nose at one puff. So he sat and looked at the Master. But Glooskap, whose pipe held ten times as much tobacco, did the same, and blowing it out split the rocky ground, so that a great chasm opened before them. Then they were silent awhile, till the Master said, 'If you can do that you may kill me.' But he could not, and so went back with shame to those who had sent him.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, p. 59; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: Glooskap Sails Through the Great Cavern of Darkness
title.zh: 格魯斯卡普舟渡黑暗巨洞

region.en: Mighty river that runs beneath the earth into the night
region.zh: 奔流地底、貫入黑夜的大河

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'How Glooskap sailed through the Great Cavern of Darkness'

summary.en: Seven neighbors of Glooskap, so many different animals, steal away his family, and he follows them to Newfoundland. Finding Marten alone he arms the boy with his belt, and the Crow spreads the news that Marten is drying meat - so a great fear falls on the town and all await death; but the Master, laughing, forgives them and gives venison, then leaves them. In a canoe with Marten and Dame Bear he sails down a mighty river: great cliffs gather round and close over them, and the river runs underground, deeper and deeper, dashing into rapids and cataracts so horrible that death seems to come and go with every plunge; Marten and the woman die of fear, but the Master sits with silent soul singing the songs of magic, passes into the night, and comes forth again into sunlight, where 'Numchahse! arise!' restores them, and Glooskap has gained the greatest power.
summary.zh: 格魯斯卡普的七位鄰居——皆為異獸——擄走其家人，他一路追至紐芬蘭。他為孤留的貂弟繫上法帶；烏鴉傳播貂弟曬肉的消息，全城大恐以待死；主人卻大笑赦免，並賜鹿肉，隨後離去。他與貂弟、熊嫗乘舟順巨流而下：絕壁合攏罩頂，大河潛入地底，愈行愈深，撞入灘石與駭人的懸瀑，每一下傾跌都似死生之交；貂弟與嫗驚懼而斃，主人卻靜坐吟唱魔法之歌，穿過長夜重見天光，一聲「起來！」喚醒二人——自此他獲得至高的力量。

sensitivity.note: Micmac tradition (Leland 1884); public domain. Leland compares the passage-underground to shamanic initiation and to the Norse river Ifing.

passages.text: Now it is told in another tradition - and men tell even this differently - that in these old times Glooskap's seven neighbors, who were all so many different animals, took away his family, and that he followed them, even as it has been written, unto Newfoundland. And when he came there it was night, and, finding Marten alone, he took him forth into the forest to seek food, putting his belt on the boy, which gave him such power that he hunted well and got much meat. So it came to pass that the next morning Dame Kah-kah-gooch, the Crow, observed that Marten was drying meat on his wigwam. And this she spread abroad. But when the people learned that the child had done this, a great fear came upon them all, and they sat every man in his lodge and awaited death, for they knew that the Master had come.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, p. 60; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: And he indeed came; but when he saw them all as frightened as rabbits before the wild-cat, he laughed aloud and forgave them, for he was noble and generous. And as they were hungry - for he had come in hard times - he gave them much venison, and sorrow departed from their wigwams. But as they had left him of old, he now left them. When they knew him not they left him to die; now that they knew him they feared lest they should perish without him. But he turned his steps towards other paths.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 61-62; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Now having made a canoe, the Master, with Marten and Dame Bear, went upon a mighty river. As the story says, it was broad and beautiful at first, and so they sailed away down towards its mouth. Then they came to great cliffs, which gathered round and closed over them. But the river ran on beneath these, and ever on far underground, deeper and deeper in the earth, till it dashed headlong into rapids, among rocks and ravines, and under cataracts which were so horrible that death seemed to come and go with every plunge of the canoe. And the water grew narrower and the current more dreadful, and fear came upon Marten and the woman, so that they died. But the Master sat with silent soul, though he sang the songs of magic, and so passed into the night, but came forth again into sunlight. And there was a lonely wigwam on the bank, into which he bore Marten and the grandmother, and saying, 'Numchahse! arise!' lo, they arose, and deemed they had only slept. And now Glooskap had gained the greatest power.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 61-62; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: The Great Works of Glooskap: The Boar's Back, Beaver Dam, and Five Islands
title.zh: 格魯斯卡普的偉蹟：豬背道、河狸壩與五島

region.en: Minas Basin and Cape Blomidon, Nova Scotia
region.zh: 新斯科舍的米納斯盆地與布洛米頓角

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'Of the Great Works which Glooskap made in the Land'

summary.en: Over all the land of the Wabanaki there is no place which was not marked by the hand of the Master. The great causeway from Cwesowralegek to Parrsborough - Ou-wokun, the Causeway, or the Boar's Back - was cast up over bogs and streams for his weary companions. The monstrous Beavers of the old time had dammed from Cape Blomidon across the Annapolis valley; Glooskap cut the great dam, and the rush of many waters swung westward and lodged with a great split - Cape Split, Pleegim, the opening of a beaver dam - while the pond left behind is the Basin of Minas. To scare the Beaver he threw handfuls of earth east of Partridge Island, which became the Five Islands; and, the Beaver having gone over the Grand Falls, he hurled a rock a hundred and fifty miles after it, which remaineth there even to this day.
summary.zh: 瓦巴納基全境無一處不見主人之手跡。自哈德伍德角至帕斯伯勒的大道——印第安名「堤道」，白人稱「豬背」——是他為疲乏的同伴在沼澤溪流之上堆起的長崗。上古巨河狸自布洛米頓角築壩攔斷安納波利斯河谷；格魯斯卡普斬開巨壩，洪水西衝，壩端留下大裂口——即「普利吉姆」、河狸壩之開口，今之斯普利特角；餘水成湖，便是米納斯盆地。為驚走河狸，他把幾把土拋到鷓鴣島以東，化作五島；河狸經大瀑而逃，他擲出一百五十里外的飛石以嚇之——此石至今猶在。

sensitivity.note: Leland 1884; public domain. Place-myth cluster of the Bay of Fundy tides and landforms.

passages.text: Over all the Land of the Wabanaki there is no place which was not marked by the hand of the Master. And it is to be seen on hills and rivers and great roads, as well as mighty rocks, which were in their day living monsters. For there is a very wonderful highway from Cwesowralegek to Parrsborough, running parallel with the river now called Hebert, and this road is called by Indians Ou-wokun, the Causeway, but by white men, or the Iglesmani, the Boar's Back. For it is said that he meant to visit Partridge Island and Cape Blomidon, but they who were with him had got tired of the sea, and wished to cross over by land. And while they were resting and getting ready for their trip across, the Master, raising his magic power to a great deed to be spoken of forever, went away a little time, and cast up a great and beautiful level ridge, throwing it over bogs and streams; and on this they traveled, rejoicing, and, having reached the island, awaited him.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 62-63; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: And yet again the Master did a mighty deed. It came to pass in those days that the Beavers had built a dam across from Utkoguncheek, or Cape Blomidon, to the opposite shore, and thereby made a pond that filled all the valley of Annapolis. Now in those times the Beavers were monstrous beasts, and the Master, though kind of heart, seems to have had but little love for them ever since the day when Qwah-beetsis, the son of the Great Beaver, tempted Malsum to slay his brother. Now the bones of these Beavers may be found to this day, and many there are on Oonamahgik, and their teeth are six inches across, and there are no such quah-beet to-day. And these are the remains of the Beavers who built the dam at Cape Blomidon and forded the Annapolis Valley.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 63-64; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Now Glooskap would have a hunt and do a deed which should equal the great whale-fishing of Kitpooseaginow. So he cut the great dam near the shore, and bade Marten watch; for he said, 'I mistrust that there is a little Beaver hiding hereabouts.' And when the dam was cut from where it joined the shore there was a mighty rush of many waters, so that it swung round to the westward, yet it did not break away from the other shore. Therefore the end of it lodged with a great split therein when the flood had found a free course, and the whole may be seen there still... and this point, or Cape Split, is called by the Micmacs Pleegim, which, being interpreted, means the opening of a beaver dam. Then, to frighten the Beaver, Glooskap threw at it a few handfuls of earth, and these, falling somewhat to the eastward of Partridge Island, became the Five Islands. And the pond which was left was the Basin of Minas.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, p. 64; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: And yet another tradition tells that, after cutting the dam, Glooskap sat and watched, but no beaver came out; for Qwah-beet had gone out of a back door. So he took a rock and threw it afar - one hundred and fifty miles - to scare the Beaver back again; but the Beaver had gone over the Grand Falls, and the stone remaineth there even to this day.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, p. 65; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: Glooskap Leaves the World: The Beasts Lose One Tongue
title.zh: 格魯斯卡普離世：群獸失其同語

region.en: Great Lake Minas, where the feast was held before his departure
region.zh: 他辭世前設宴的米納斯大湖

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'How Glooskap, leaving the World, all the Animals mourned for him'

summary.en: Glooskap had freed the world from the mighty monsters of an early time - giants, the cullo, the dreadful Chenoo of the North - and taught men the arts which made them happier; but they were not grateful, and though they worshiped him they were not the less wicked. When the ways of men and beasts waxed evil they greatly vexed Glooskap, and he made a rich feast by the shore of the great Lake Minas; when the feast was over he got into a great canoe, and the beasts looked after him till they saw him no more, still hearing his voice as he sang, fainter and fainter - and then deep silence fell, and the beasts, who had till now spoken but one language, were no longer able to understand each other, and fled each his own way. Until the day when Glooskap shall return to restore the Golden Age all Nature mourns: the Great Snowy Owl repeats to the night 'Koo-koo-skoos!' - Oh, I am sorry! - and the Loons go restlessly up and down through the world seeking vainly for their master.
summary.zh: 格魯斯卡普已為世間清除上古的巨怪——巨人、庫洛巨鳥、北方可怖的食人鬼——並教人技藝使其安樂；然人心不感其恩，雖崇拜他卻依然作惡。當人獸之行日益敗壞，主人再也忍受不住，便在米納斯大湖畔設下盛宴。宴罷他登上巨舟，群獸目送他直至不見；歌聲漸遠漸微，終歸死寂——而一直同語的群獸從此再聽不懂彼此，各自四散奔逃。直到格魯斯卡普歸來、重開黃金時代的之日，萬物皆哀：大雪鴞入林夜啼「庫庫斯庫斯！」——唉，我難過！——而忠於他的潛鳥們在世上往復徘徊，尋主不獲，悲鳴不已。

sensitivity.note: Micmac tradition (Leland 1884); public domain. A Babel-style ending and a millennial return prophecy.

passages.text: Now Glooskap had freed the world from all the mighty monsters of an early time: the giants wandered no longer in the wilderness; the cullo terrified man no more, as it spread its wings like the cloud between him and the sun; the dreadful Chenoo of the North devoured him not; no evil beasts, devils, and serpents were to be found near his home. And the Master had, moreover, taught men the arts which made them happier; but they were not grateful to him, and though they worshiped him they were not the less wicked.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 66-67; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: 'Now when the ways of men and beasts waxed evil they greatly vexed Glooskap, and at length he could no longer endure them, and he made a rich feast by the shore of the great Lake Minas. All the beasts came to it, and when the feast was over he got into a great canoe, and the beasts looked after him till they saw him no more. And after they ceased to see him, they still heard his voice as he sang; but the sounds grew fainter and fainter in the distance, and at last they wholly died away; and then deep silence fell on them all, and a great marvel came to pass, and the beasts, who had till now spoken but one language, were no longer able to understand each other, and they fled away, each his own way, and never again have they met together in council. Until the day when Glooskap shall return to restore the Golden Age, and make men and animals dwell once more together in amity and peace, all Nature mourns.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 67-68; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: And tradition says that on his departure from Acadia the Great Snowy Owl retired to the deep forests, to return no more until he could come to welcome Glooskap; and in those sylvan depths the owls even yet repeat to the night 'Koo-koo-skoos!' which is to say in the Indian tongue, 'Oh, I am sorry! Oh, I am sorry!' And the Loons, who had been the huntsmen of Glooskap, go restlessly up and down through the world, seeking vainly for their master, whom they cannot find, and wailing sadly because they find him not. But ere the Master went away from life... he bade it be made known by the Loons, his faithful messengers, that before his departure years would pass, and that whoever would seek him might have one wish granted, whatever that wish might be.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 68-69; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: The Three Seekers: The Magic Pipe, the Bag of Women, and the Root
title.zh: 三位求願者：魔法笛、女人之袋與奇根

region.en: The long road to Glooskap's dwelling, and Old Town, Maine
region.zh: 通往格魯斯卡普居所的長路，與緬因老鎮

texts.period: Told in the tent of John Gabriel, Passamaquoddy (Leland 1884)

source.work: Charles G. Leland, The Algonquin Legends of New England (1884), 'Of other Men who went to Glooskap for Gifts'

summary.en: When all men heard that Glooskap would grant a wish to any one who would come to him, three Indians - a Maliseet and two Penobscots - resolved to try, and were seven years on the road. The honest bad hunter receives the magic pipe that persuades every animal to follow its player; the second, whose heart is set on the love of many women, receives a tightly tied bag with the warning not to open it till home - he opens it in the woods, and hundreds of beautiful girls, wild with passion, swarm about him until, panting and crying for breath, he perishes; and the foolish merry fellow who wants the marvelous laughing-sound eats the magic root on the road - it answers perfectly, in the woods and among the people - until he grows weary of himself, goes into the woods and slays himself, and Bumole, the evil spirit of the night-air, bears him away to Lahmekqu, the dwelling place of darkness.
summary.zh: 傳聞格魯斯卡普許願於來訪者，三位印第安人（一米克馬利特、二佩諾布斯科特）踏上七年長路。誠實而拙於狩獵者得魔法笛——笛聲所至，百獸相隨；求「女人越多越好」者得一繫緊的袋子，囑其到家再開——他半路啟袋，數百黑眸長髮的美女如白鴿湧出，熱情擁吻，愈聚愈多，他喘息求饒不得，終被窒息而死；求「奇妙笑聲」的輕浮少年半路吞下魔法之根——聲響妙極，卻在獵鹿時不受控制地爆出，嚇走獵物；族人漸厭，他厭倦自己，入林自盡——夜氣之惡靈布穆勒自雲端降下，攜他往黑暗的居所。

passages.text: When all men had heard that Glooskap would grant a wish to any one who would come to him, three Indians resolved to try this thing; and one was a Maliseet from St. John, and the other two were Penobscots from Old Town. And the path was long and the way was hard, and they suffered much, and they were seven years on it ere they came to him. But while they were yet three months' journey from his dwelling, they heard the barking of his dogs, and as they drew nearer, day by day, it was louder. And so, after great trials, they found the lord of men and beasts, and he made them welcome and entertained them. But, ere they went, he asked them what they wanted.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 69-70; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: And the eldest, who was an honest, simple man, and of but little account among his people, because he was a bad hunter, asked that he might excel in the killing and catching of game. Then the Master gave him a flute, or the magic pipe, which pleases every ear, and has the power of persuading every animal to follow him who plays it. Now the second Indian, being asked what he would have, replied, The love of many women... At hearing this the Master seemed displeased, but, smiling anon, he gave him a bag which was tightly tied, and told him not to open it until he had reached his home. Now the third Indian was a gay and handsome but foolish young fellow, whose whole heart was set on making people laugh; and he said that it would please him most to be able to make a certain quaint and marvelous sound or noise... And to him Glooskap was also affable, sending Marten into the woods to seek a certain mystical and magic root, which when eaten would make the miracle the young man sought. But he warned him not to touch the root ere he got to his home, or it would be the worse for him.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 70-71; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: It had taken seven years to come, but seven days were all that was required to tread the path returning to their home, that is, for him who got there. Only one of all the three beheld his lodge again... But he who loved women, and had never won even a wife, was filled with anxious wishfulness. And he had not gone very far into the woods before he opened the bag. And there flew out by hundreds, like white doves, swarming all about him, beautiful girls, with black burning eyes and flowing hair. And wild with passion the winsome witches threw their arms about him, and kissed him as he responded to their embraces; but they came ever more and more, wilder and more passionate. And he bade them give way, but they would not, and he sought to escape, but he could not; and so panting, crying for breath, smothered, he perished. And those who came that way found him dead, but what became of the girls no man knows.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 71-72; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Now the third went merrily onward alone, when all at once it flashed upon his mind that Glooskap had given him a present, and without the least heed to the injunction... drew out the root and ate it; and scarce had he done this ere he realized that he possessed the power of uttering the weird and mystic sound to absolute perfection. And as it rang o'er many a hill and dale... he felt that it was indeed wonderful. So he walked on gayly, trumpeting as he went, over hill and vale, happy as a bird. But by and by he began to weary of himself. Seeing a deer he drew an arrow and stealing silently to the game was just about to shoot, when despite himself the wild, unearthly sound broke forth like a demon's warble. The deer bounded away, and the young man cursed! And when he reached Old Town, half dead with hunger, he was worth little to make laughter, though the honest Indians at first did not fail to do so... But as the days went on they wearied of him, and, life becoming a burden, he went into the woods and slew himself. And the evil spirit of the night-air, even Bumole, or Pamola, from whom came the gift, swooped down from the clouds and bore him away to Lahmekqu, the dwelling place of darkness, and he was no more heard of among men.
passages.note: Verbatim from Leland 1884, pp. 71-72; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
